title: Making a Will to Leave a House and Land: Valid Forms and Key Notes
desc: What makes a will leaving a house and land valid: handwritten, witnessed or notarized, mandatory content, and who still inherits even if not named in the will.
summary: A guide to making a will leaving a house and land under the Civil Code 2015: forms of will, mandatory content, witnesses, notarization and heirs who inherit regardless of the will.
body: p

Making a will lets parents decide for themselves who receives the house and land, avoiding disputes among their children and grandchildren later. But a will written in the wrong form may be treated as invalid, in which case the house and land are divided by law instead (Article 650 of the Civil Code).
h2
1. Who may make a will?
p

An adult who is of sound mind and clear judgment and is not deceived, threatened or coerced has the right to make a will. A person aged from 15 to under 18 may make a will if a parent or guardian consents (Article 625).
h2
2. Forms of will
p
A will must be made in writing; only when it is impossible to make one in writing may an oral will be made (Article 627). Written wills fall into 4 types (Article 628):
ul
Without witnesses: the testator must write it by hand and sign the will (Article 633).

With witnesses: if not handwritten, it may be typed or written by another person, but there must be at least two witnesses; the testator signs or fingerprints in front of them and they sign to confirm (Article 634).
Notarized or certified (Article 635); made at a notarial practice organization or the commune-level People's Committee following the procedure in Article 636.
p

An oral will is valid only when the testator expresses their final wishes before at least two witnesses, who record it and sign or fingerprint immediately, and within 05 working days a notary or competent authority must certify the signatures or fingerprints of the witnesses (Clause 5, Article 630).
h2
3. Mandatory content and how to write it
p
Under Article 631, a will contains the following main contents:
ol
The day, month and year the will is made;
The full name and place of residence of the testator;
The full name of the person, agency or organization receiving the estate;
The estate left and where it is located (it is advisable to state the certificate number, land plot number, and the address of the house and land).
p

A will must not use abbreviations or symbols; if it has several pages, each page must be numbered and signed or fingerprinted by the testator; any erasure or correction must be signed beside it by the person who wrote the will or by the witnesses.
h2
4. Who may not act as a witness?
p

Under Article 632, the following may not act as witnesses: a person who inherits under the will or by law from the testator; a person with property rights or obligations related to the content of the will; a minor, a person who has lost civil act capacity, or a person with difficulty in cognition or controlling their behavior. Therefore, children and grandchildren who receive the house should not act as witnesses.
p
If the testator is physically impaired or illiterate, the will must be written down by a witness and notarized or certified (Clause 3, Article 630).
h2
5. People who still inherit even if not named
p

Under Article 644, minor children, parents, a spouse, and adult children who are unable to work still receive a share of the estate equal to two-thirds of a share of a statutory heir, if the will gives them nothing or less than that – unless they refuse to accept or have no right to inherit. When disposing of a house and land, this portion should be accounted for in advance to avoid disputes.
h2
6. Notarization, safekeeping and amending the will
ul

Notarizing a will: the testator may not authorize another person but must sign personally, or sign and fingerprint; the notary refuses if the testator shows signs of having lost civil act capacity or of being deceived, threatened or coerced (Article 58 of the Notarization Law 2024).
The will may be deposited with a notarial practice organization for safekeeping; the notary seals it in front of the testator and issues a receipt of deposit (Article 61).
The testator may amend, supplement, replace or revoke the will at any time; if there are several wills for the same property, only the last one is effective (Article 640; Clause 5, Article 643).

Notarizing a will is an exception and is not limited to the province where the notarial organization has its office, unlike other real estate transactions (Article 44 of the Notarization Law 2024; Law 04/2026/QH16, which amends this article from 1 January 2027, still keeps the exception for wills).
p
A will takes effect only from the time the succession opens (Clause 1, Article 643); while they are alive, the parents retain full rights over their own house and land.
note

This article is a summary for reference and does not replace legal documents. The Notarization Law 2024 has been amended by Law 106/2025/QH15 (not yet in our library) and Law 04/2026/QH16 (effective 1 January 2027). If the house and land are the spouses' common property, each person can dispose of only their own share. It is advisable to make a notarized will to limit disputes.
